notes: Permission and case-management order in paternity appeal; remittal and consolidated section 55A hearing are clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Re J: paternity appeal permission with remitted section 55A proceedings
key_facts: The applicant sought permission to appeal in family proceedings founded on the assertion that the younger child was not his biological child.
Parallel section 55A non-parentage proceedings had been issued in Swindon County Court but lay dormant until late service and were adjourned by consent.
The child A was approaching 15 and the court expressed concern about his position in the proceedings.
Reporting restrictions were imposed restricting identification to initials pending the adjourned appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Oral permission application in the Court of Appeal with appeal to follow if granted; appeal adjourned generally pending consolidated High Court determination.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted; section 55A proceedings elevated to the High Court for a consolidated hearing with the remitted issue of whether the respondent presented a false paternity case years earlier; appeal adjourned with costs reserved.
enrichment.ratio: Where the success of a family appeal depends on resolving disputed paternity, an appellate court may grant permission but refer the factual investigation to a judge of the Division under CPR 52.10(2)(b) rather than determine credibility itself; section 55A best-interests and FLRA 1969 sampling issues should be heard together with the remitted false-case issue.
legal_issues: Whether permission to appeal should be granted on disputed paternity
Which court should determine disputed parentage and credibility
Whether consolidated section 55A and remitted proceedings were appropriate
Whether the child should be separately represented

confidence.notes: Interlocutory case-management order only; merits of paternity and appeal outcome remain undetermined.

notes: Detailed coroner jury and Article 2 inquest challenge; Peach test and adequacy of inquiry clearly analysed.

enrichment.short_title: Takoushis: coroner jury refusal and psychiatric A&E inquest challenge
key_facts: Pavlos Takoushis, a long-term schizophrenic voluntary patient, absconded from Chase Farm Hospital and was taken to St Thomas' A&E after attempting to jump from Tower Bridge.
Triaged as category 2 high self-harm risk, he was left alone and absconded again before psychiatric assessment; his body was found in the Thames five weeks later.
The coroner refused a jury under section 8(3)(d) and declined to adjourn for independent expert evidence on A&E protocols.
The inquest returned a verdict of suicide, rejecting neglect contributed to by systemic failings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a completed coroner's inquest seeking quashing and a fresh jury inquest.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the coroner erred in treating absconding as atypical on the Peach first limb but was entitled to find no defective system requiring a jury on the second limb; refusal of family expert evidence was within discretion.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 8(3)(d) a jury is mandatory only where the coroner has reason to suspect death occurred in recurring systemic circumstances that reasonable measures could prevent; an individual delay in implementing an otherwise reasonable triage system does not suffice, and an inquest need not admit family experts where systemic failure is not in issue.
legal_issues: Whether section 8(3)(d) required a jury for voluntary psychiatric patients absconding from A&E
Application of the Peach two-limb test for jury summoning
Whether the inquest inquiry was Article 2 compliant and sufficient
Whether the coroner should have permitted independent expert evidence
linked_authorities: R v Her Majesty's Coroner at Hammersmith, ex parte Peach [1980] QB 211
R (Middleton) v West Somerset Coroner [2004] UKHL 10
R (Amin) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] UKHL 51

confidence.notes: Full substantive judgment on both grounds with clear application of established coroner authorities.

notes: IAT permission JR on Articles 3 and 8; flawed destitution reasoning and Mahmood family-life analysis are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Doka: quashing IAT refusal of leave on Articles 3 and 8
key_facts: Mrs Doka, a Sudanese woman nearly 65, entered the UK on a visitor visa and later claimed asylum, living with her refugee daughter and grandchildren in the UK.
The adjudicator dismissed her asylum and human rights claims; the IAT refused permission to appeal in September 2003.
The adjudicator assumed UK-based children would support her in Sudan without evidence she could open a bank account or receive remittances there.
Her UK children could not safely return to Sudan because of political persecution risks accepted when they were granted asylum.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal of permission to appeal, following renewed leave limited to Articles 3 and 8.
enrichment.outcome: IAT refusal of leave quashed; the Article 3 conclusion involved an improper factual jump on destitution and the Article 8 analysis under Mahmood was arguably wrong given insurmountable obstacles to family reunion in Sudan.
enrichment.ratio: On judicial review of an IAT leave refusal, an arguable error of law suffices; inferring absence of destitution on return from children's willingness to pay, without proof remittances could be received, is flawed, and Article 8 may resist removal where family life exists in the UK and refugee children cannot safely relocate to the country of origin.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator's Article 3 destitution finding was supported by evidence
Whether Article 8 family life existed despite prior separation from UK children
Application of Mahmood on insurmountable obstacles to family life abroad
Standard for granting leave to appeal on human rights grounds
linked_authorities: Mahmood v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2001] UKHRR 307
Bensaid v United Kingdom (2001) 33 EHRR 10
Razgar v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] UKHL 27

notes: Leading asylum statutory review authority; proportionality and Article 14 analysis are comprehensive.

enrichment.short_title: M and G v IAT: statutory review replaces parallel judicial review
key_facts: Iranian and Zimbabwean asylum seekers were refused permission to appeal to the IAT and sought both statutory review under section 101 and judicial review on the same grounds.
Collins J held parallel judicial review an abuse of process after failed statutory review but granted permission on renewal for these conjoined appeals.
Section 101 provides paper-only High Court review with no further appeal, designed to expedite asylum challenges.
Parliament intended statutory review as a proportionate substitute for multi-stage judicial review with oral hearings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Conjoined Court of Appeal appeals from Collins J's dismissal of judicial review as abuse of process after statutory review.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; pursuing judicial review on grounds already or potentially raised in statutory review is a proper exercise of discretion and Article 14 discrimination is not made out.
enrichment.ratio: Where section 101 provides a satisfactory alternative remedy, the Administrative Court may refuse judicial review of an IAT leave refusal as an abuse of process; paper statutory review by an experienced judge is proportionate given the two-tier tribunal system, and differential treatment of asylum applicants is objectively justified.
legal_issues: Whether judicial review remains available after failed section 101 statutory review
Whether statutory review without an oral hearing is a proportionate remedy
Whether restricting asylum seekers to paper review infringes Article 14 ECHR
Relationship between CPR 54.25 and section 101
linked_authorities: R (Sivasubramaniam) v Wandsworth County Court [2002] EWCA Civ 1738
Sengupta v Holmes [2002] EWCA Civ 1104
Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza [2004] UKHL 30

enrichment.short_title: Head v Orrow: sentence reduced for non-molestation order breach
key_facts: The appellant was found in contempt for three breaches of a non-molestation order protecting his child's grandmother Mrs O.
On 21 June 2004 he blocked Mrs O's path, grabbed her throat and forced her onto a car bonnet in a public street.
He contested the committal, was disbelieved with his alibi witness, and showed no remorse.
HH Judge Sleeman sentenced him to 12 months immediate imprisonment for the principal breach.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence following committal for breach of a section 42 Family Law Act 1996 non-molestation order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; total sentence reduced from 12 months to 9 months immediate imprisonment, with concurrent 6 months for a lesser breach unchanged.
enrichment.ratio: Sentences for contempt under section 42 should reflect contemporary deterrence for domestic violence and align where possible with Protection from Harassment Act and Crown Court assault sentencing, but a 12-month term was excessive for a first offence of this kind absent concurrent criminal proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether 12 months immediate imprisonment was manifestly excessive
Application of Hale v Tanner guidance on section 42 committal sentencing
Relationship between family contempt sentences and criminal harassment sentencing
Whether desire for contact with a child was mitigating
linked_authorities: Hale v Tanner [2000] 2 FLR 879
Lomas v Parle [2003] EWCA Civ 1804
Re L (Contact: Domestic Violence) [2001] Fam 260

enrichment.short_title: R v Mitchell: section 41 rape appeal dismissed

statutes_considered.title: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999

key_facts: Raymond Mitchell was convicted by a 10-2 majority of rape after approaching a woman near Hagley Road Birmingham with a kitchen knife.
The defence case was consensual paid sex with a prostitute; the prosecution relied on the knife, threats and DNA.
The trial judge limited cross-examination on the complainant's prostitution activity two days earlier under section 41.
Prosecution witness Andrew Steer did not attend; trial proceeded by agreement without his recent complaint evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction for rape with leave of the full court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; restriction of section 41(5) cross-examination about prostitution on 21 June did not render the conviction unsafe, and proceeding without Steer was a tenable trial decision.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 41(5), prior prostitution evidence may rebut prosecution evidence about a sabbatical from sex work, but a judge may properly exclude earlier activity as going further than necessary for a fair trial where same-day evidence already addresses the issue; agreeing to proceed without a recent-complaint witness does not undermine safety where counsel's judgment was reasonable.
legal_issues: Whether section 41(5) required cross-examination about prostitution on 21 June 2001
Whether the judge's section 41 ruling was unduly restrictive
Whether proceeding without Andrew Steer rendered the trial unfair
Whether conviction was safe despite disputed consent
linked_authorities: R v A (No 2) [2002] 2 Crim App R 351
Clinton (1993) 97 Cr App R 320

confidence.notes: Both grounds analysed in detail with clear safety conclusion.

enrichment.short_title: R v Taylor: cannabis factory sentence reduced for disparity
key_facts: Taylor and Hattersley were convicted of conspiracy to produce Class B cannabis at a professional hydroponic factory yielding about £50,000 per month.
Taylor was a qualified electrician who bypassed the electricity supply; Hattersley had no convictions and Taylor was treated as of good character.
Co-accused Doman, with a substantial record, was sentenced to 8 years at trial but reduced to 7 years on appeal.
Taylor and Hattersley each received 7 years, one year less than Doman only because of their good character.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence returned to the Court of Appeal by the Criminal Cases Review Commission after Doman's sentence was reduced.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; sentences quashed and substituted with 6 years' imprisonment to preserve the trial judge's good-character distinction after Doman's reduction to 7 years.
enrichment.ratio: Where a trial judge deliberately sentenced co-defendants of equal culpability differently only because of previous convictions, reducing the worse-record defendant's sentence as too high requires a corresponding reduction for the better-character defendants to avoid apparent injustice.
legal_issues: Whether disparity with co-defendant Doman warranted sentence reduction
Appropriate level of sentence for large-scale cannabis production
Effect of CCRC reference on disparity arguments
Whether good character mitigation should be reflected after Doman's appeal

R v Chamberlain [1998] 1 Cr App R(S) 49
R v Sykes [1982] Cr App R(S) 173

enrichment.short_title: W v Wandsworth IAP: permanent exclusion for knife upheld
key_facts: Pupil M at Nightingale School was permanently excluded for possessing a knife on school premises under a zero-tolerance Behaviour Management Policy.
M claimed he found the knife under stairs and was handing it in; staff saw him conceal it and pretend to dispose of it before eventually surrendering it to the school secretary.
The governors' panel and Wandsworth Independent Appeal Panel upheld permanent exclusion after finding he did not intend to hand the knife in when first challenged.
M had a Statement of Special Educational Needs; DfES guidance cautioned against excluding statemented pupils except in exceptional circumstances.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Owen J's refusal of judicial review of an independent appeal panel decision upholding permanent exclusion.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the IAP lawfully found M was not intending to hand in the knife and permanent exclusion was a rational response; supplementary chair evidence was admissible and supported by contemporaneous notes.
enrichment.ratio: An independent appeal panel may uphold a strict weapons policy exclusion where it finds the pupil possessed a knife and did not hand it over when first asked, even if the pupil later claimed an innocent purpose; ex post facto panel chair evidence explaining deliberations is admissible if not mere rationalisation, and DfES guidance on statemented pupils was considered.
legal_issues: Whether the IAP decided solely on policy without assessing proportionality
Whether the IAP made adequate findings that M did not intend to hand in the knife
Admissibility and reliability of supplementary IAP chair evidence
Whether permanent exclusion was irrational given special educational needs
linked_authorities: R (Ermakov) v Westminster City Council [1996] 2 All ER 302
R (D) v Northamptonshire County Council [1998] ED CR 14

notes: Landmark hospital-death Article 2 inquest JR; Powell/Sieminska analysis and expert evidence discretion are thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Goodson v Coroner: ERCP death inquest and Article 2
key_facts: Harry Coleman, 83, died after an elective ERCP at Luton and Dunstable Hospital caused a rare duodenal perforation; conservative management preceded fatal cardiac arrest.
The coroner held an inquest without a jury, refused to treat it as an Article 2 investigation, and declined to instruct an independent medical expert.
Evidence came mainly from the operating surgeon Miss Cheslyn-Curtis and specialist registrar Dr Gupta, cross-examined by the family's solicitor.
The verdict was death by misadventure; the family later obtained independent expert reports not relied on in this judicial review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a completed inquest challenging refusal of Article 2 scope and refusal to instruct independent expert evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; Article 2 procedural obligation was not engaged on mere potential negligence, and even if engaged the inquest was an effective independent investigation without independent clinical experts on these facts.
enrichment.ratio: Simple medical negligence causing death in NHS care does not engage the separate Article 2 procedural duty to investigate; where only negligence is in issue an inquest need not call independent experts if the coroner reasonably considers treating clinicians' evidence and hospital records sufficient, and civil negligence remedies form part of the overall judicial system under Powell and Calvelli.
legal_issues: Whether Article 2 required an enhanced inquest into hospital ERCP death
Whether the coroner unlawfully refused independent medical expert evidence
Distinction between positive and procedural Article 2 obligations in medical negligence
Whether the inquest complied with Jordan minimum criteria
linked_authorities: R (Middleton) v West Somerset Coroner [2004] UKHL 10
Powell v United Kingdom (2000) 30 EHRR CD 362
Jordan v United Kingdom (2001) 37 EHRR 52

confidence.notes: Substantive reserved judgment on Article 2 scope and expert evidence with clear dismissal.

notes: Important DDA education comparator ruling; inadequacy of SENDIST reasons and Ermakov remission refusal clearly explained.

enrichment.short_title: VK v Norfolk: SENDIST disability discrimination decision quashed
key_facts: Disabled pupil JS received no education for months after moving to Norfolk, then only 1.75 hours weekly visiting teacher support before a school placement.
His mother claimed Norfolk County Council discriminated under the DDA in its section 19 educational provision pending placement.
The SENDIST compared JS with other VTS pupils rather than mainstream school pupils and gave inadequate reasons on justification.
JS had neurodevelopmental disorder, weak literacy and numeracy, but above-average conceptual language skills.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on point of law from a SENDIST disability discrimination decision dismissing the claim.
enrichment.outcome: Tribunal decision quashed for wrong comparator under section 28B, possible misdirection on 'solely' relating to disability, and inadequate justification reasons; remission to supplement reasons refused under Ermakov principles.
enrichment.ratio: Less favourable treatment of a disabled child unable to attend school must be compared with ordinary pupils receiving mainstream education, not with other visiting-teacher pupils; breach of section 19 does not automatically constitute DDA discrimination but resources may be a material substantial justification if adequately reasoned; SENDIST reasons must stand on the written decision and cannot normally be supplemented later.
legal_issues: Correct comparator for section 28B discrimination in section 19 education
Whether treatment must relate solely or only partly to disability
Adequacy of SENDIST reasons on justification
Whether resources can justify less favourable VTS provision
linked_authorities: Clark v TDG Ltd (trading as Novacold) [1999] IRLR 318
McA Catholic High School v CC [2003] EWHC 3045 (Admin)
R (Ermakov) v Westminster City Council [1996] 2 All ER 302
